doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Parker's records change his path
summary: Hearing Parker made him want to be a professional musician; his asthmatic condition was helped by horn playing.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: By this time, were you listening more regularly to records...
Well, they didn’t have many records. They had but one or two records, “Jumpin’ The Blues” by Jay McShann...
Oh, yeah. I’d listen to anything that I figured was jazz. But I wasn’t a record addict, because I didn’t really want to hear anything but what he was playing, and once I heard him...
So based on “The Jumpin’ Blues” by Charlie Parker with McShann, it changed your...
Yeah, that changed everything. Not me. Everybody.
Talk about how it changed you. What did it do?

Well, it made me want to pursue music as a profession. Because actually, when I went to college, as I told you, I was an honor roll—I was planning to go on to probably pre law school or something. My parents wanted me to do something else. Because I was asthmatic, and they figured that playing a horn is the latest thing they’d want you to do. But they were wrong, because playing the horn actually made me survive. The diaphragm, breathing, and stuff like that; it made my lungs much stronger than weaker. That’s what it made for me.
